solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

passage_notes: Historical/technical claims check out: acoustic recording until c. 1925 (Western Electric electrical process adopted 1925); tuba substituted for string bass; Stroh-type horn violin; pianos raised close to horn; ~3 min per side of a 10-inch 78; symphonies split across sides, sometimes at quicker tempos; microphone enabling crooning. minor: 'slowly turning disc' is loose for ~78 rpm (slow only relative to later expectations, arguably fine). Passage is clear and ACT-appropriate.

flags: minor: D is a defensible-sounding partial (paragraph 2 only) but clearly too narrow; A and C are extreme reversals that few will pick, so effectively a 2-choice item
minor: choices A and C preview the answers to R029-06 (records are not worthless) and R029-08 (electrical recording did not free performers to sound exactly like themselves)
R029-01.notes: Thesis: records are a 'negotiation' between players and device; B captures both halves. A contradicts para 5; C contradicts para 6; D too narrow.

flags: minor: answer cue - key copies passage wording ('blunter tone', 'carried better') almost verbatim
minor: B borrows the violin description and C the singer description; A is the only real trap (low notes)
R029-02.notes: Para 3: 'replaced it with a tuba, whose blunter tone carried better.'

R029-03.notes: Hybrid violin illustrates lengths taken to suit the horn. C is a reversal trap (horn disfavored scattered sound); B, D off-topic.

flags: minor: A and D are throwaway literal senses few will pick; B is the only plausible distractor
R029-04.notes: Players adjusted to a device with its own preferences, later 'learned to play to it' -> mutual adjustment.

flags: minor: answer cue - key closely paraphrases the passage sentence (project; step back on loudest notes)
minor: overlaps with R029-02 as a second para-3 detail item
R029-05.notes: Labeled as inference ('most likely') but is direct restatement of para 3 last sentence. B reversal, C contradicts low-note claim, D confuses time limit.

flags: minor: R029-01 choice A ('too distorted ... to be of any use to historians') signals that para 5's role is to rebut that idea, partly cueing this item
R029-06.notes: 'None of this means that early records are worthless as evidence' -> qualifies the distortion account. A describes para 6; D contradicts; C wrong paragraph. 'Qualify' vocabulary may trip some students.

flags: 'say little about the players' taste' is somewhat stronger than the passage supports: para 4 says only 'sometimes ... a little quicker', and para 5 insists records preserve real details. The hedge 'may be quicker' rescues it, and the other choices are clearly wrong, so it remains the single best answer, but consider softening to 'may not reliably show the tempos the players preferred'.
minor: the 'taste' wording borrows from the para 5 singer sentence, a mild synthesis that helps careful readers
R029-07.notes: Para 4: tempos 'a little quicker than they would have chosen in a concert'. A is the main trap (takes records at face value); B unsupported (warping not mentioned); D reverses quicker->slower.

flags: minor: answer cue - 'Yet microphones had preferences too' immediately follows the quoted claim, so the key is almost a restatement
R029-08.notes: Author raises the claim as 'tempting' then rebuts it. C overstates (no claim about accuracy); B reverses; D false.

flags: minor: A and C (faithful copying/restoration) both embody the 'window' view the passage rejects and are parallel, so a test-taker can eliminate them as a pair; B is weak
R029-09.notes: Performers tailored delivery to the device rather than the listener in the room; D's camera vs. room mirrors that exactly.
